zh:
四、明治愚癡多病，如經中說：「愚癡多者，教觀因緣。」問曰：因緣之法，其義甚深，云何愚癡之人教觀因緣？答曰：言愚癡者，非謂如牛、羊等，但是人聰明利根，分別籌量，不得正慧，邪心取理，名為愚癡。愚癡之病既有三種，對治亦應立三：一、明治斷常癡病者，邪思執著，或起常見，或起斷見，便破因果，病相如前說。對治方法，應教觀三世十二因緣，過去有二，現在有八，未來有二，是為十二因緣。三世相因，不常不斷，如經偈說：
我真佛法中，雖空亦不斷，
相續亦不常，善惡亦不失。
若行者能善觀十二因緣，不執斷常，則邪見心息，亦得以此對治，破相續假惑。
en: Fourth, clarifying the treatment for one whose ailment is much delusion: as the sūtra says, "One with much delusion should be taught to contemplate causation." Question: the dharma of causation is exceedingly profound in its meaning — how, then, can a deluded person be taught to contemplate causation at all? Answer: what is meant here by "delusion" does not refer to something like an ox or a sheep; rather, it refers to a person of genuine intelligence and sharp faculties who nonetheless, in discriminating and reasoning things through, fails to attain right wisdom, seizing upon principle instead with a deviant mind — this is what is called delusion. Since the ailment of delusion is itself of three kinds, its antidote should likewise be established in three forms.

First, treating the delusion of holding to annihilationism or eternalism: deviant thought clings fixedly, giving rise to either the view of eternalism or the view of annihilationism, thereby breaking apart cause and effect — the mark of this ailment is exactly as described above. The antidote method should teach the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination across the three periods of time: two links belong to the past, eight to the present, and two to the future — these together are the twelve links. Causing one another across the three periods of time, they are neither permanent nor cut off, exactly as the sūtra verse says:
"Within my own true Buddhadharma, though empty, it is nonetheless not cut off;
Continuing on, it is nonetheless not permanent; the wholesome and unwholesome are nonetheless never lost."
If the practitioner is able to properly contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination, clinging neither to annihilationism nor to eternalism, the mind of wrong view comes to rest — and this may likewise serve as the antidote breaking through the delusion of provisional reality established by continuity.

zh: 二、明治計有無癡病發者，邪念思惟有我無我、有陰無陰等，如前說。立對治者，應教觀果報十二因緣。果報十二因緣者，觀現在歌羅邏時，名曰無明，乃至生老死等。現在即有五陰、十二入、十八界成就，皆從因緣生。此歌羅邏時，即有三事：一、命；二、暖；三、識，故名無明。此既從緣而生，無有自性，不可言有，不可言無，乃至老死亦復如是。若知非空非有，即破空、有二見。當知果報十二因緣觀，即治有無見病，今亦得以此對治，破執因成假惑。三、明治世性愚癡發者，若見細微之性能生萬法，如是邪念，名計世性，廣說如前。對治之法，還作一念十二緣觀。何以故？行者深觀一念之中具足十二，一非十二，十二非一，而今約一說十二，約十二說一。當知一無定性，無定一故，則世性不可得，故以一念十二緣觀破執世性邪癡。此一念十二緣觀多破執一異見，今亦即得以此破相待假惑。
en: Second, treating the delusion of holding to existence or nonexistence arising: deviant thought reflects on whether a self exists or does not exist, whether the aggregates exist or do not exist, and so on, exactly as described above. To establish its antidote, one should be taught the contemplation of the twelve links as karmic result. The twelve links as karmic result are contemplated thus: observing that, at the present moment of kalala, this is named ignorance, on through birth, old age, and death; in the present, the five aggregates, the twelve sense-bases, and the eighteen elements are already complete, all arisen from causes and conditions. At the very moment of kalala, there are already three things present: life-force, warmth, and consciousness — hence it is named ignorance. Since this arises entirely from conditions, it has no nature of its own; it cannot be said to exist, and it cannot be said not to exist — and the same holds all the way through to old age and death as well. Knowing that it is neither empty nor existent breaks through the two views of emptiness and existence. One should know that the contemplation of the twelve links as karmic result serves precisely to treat the ailment of the view of existence or nonexistence — and this may likewise serve as the antidote breaking through the delusion of provisional reality established by cause.

Third, treating the delusion of holding to a fixed worldly nature arising: seeing some subtle, fundamental nature as able to give rise to the ten thousand dharmas — such a deviant notion is called holding to a fixed worldly nature, described at length above. Its antidote method returns instead to the contemplation of the twelve links within a single thought-moment. Why is this? The practitioner deeply contemplates that, within a single thought-moment, all twelve links are already present in full: the one is not the twelve, and the twelve are not the one, and yet, here, the twelve are spoken of in terms of the one, and the one is spoken of in terms of the twelve. One should know that the one has no fixed nature of its own — and, since there is no fixed "one," no fixed worldly nature can be found either. Hence the contemplation of the twelve links within a single thought-moment breaks through the deviant delusion of holding to a fixed worldly nature. This same contemplation of the twelve links within a single thought-moment is, moreover, especially effective at breaking through the view that clings to sameness or difference — and this, too, may serve as the antidote breaking through the delusion of provisional reality established by mutual dependence.

zh: 五、明治惡業障道多病，如經中說：「障道者，教令念佛。」今障道既有三種，對治則亦立三：一、明治沈昏闇塞障發者，惡業病相，如前說。對治，應教觀應佛三十二相中隨取一相，或先取佛眉間毫相，閉目而觀。若心闇鈍，懸作不成，當對一好端嚴形像，一心取相，緣之入定。若不明了，即開眼更觀，復更閉目。如是取一相明了，次第遍觀眾相，使心眼開明，即破昏睡沈闇之心，念佛功德則除罪障。問曰：若取其相分明，能破沈昏者，何不作九想白骨等觀？答曰：九想白骨但是生死不淨之身，除罪義劣，故非對治。
en: Fifth, clarifying the treatment for one whose ailment is much unwholesome karma obstructing the path: as the sūtra says, "One whose path is obstructed should be taught to recollect the Buddha." Since the path's obstruction is itself of three kinds, its antidote should likewise be established in three forms.

First, treating the obstruction of sunken, dark dullness arising: the mark of this unwholesome-karma ailment is as described above. Its antidote should teach taking up, from among the thirty-two marks of the response-body buddha, any single mark as its object — perhaps first taking the mark of the tuft of hair between the Buddha's brows, closing the eyes and contemplating it. If the mind is too dull and dark to sustain this without any physical support, one should instead face a fine, dignified image, single-mindedly taking up its mark as the object through which concentration is entered. If it remains unclear, one should open the eyes and look again, then close them once more — taking up a single mark in this way until it becomes clear, then, in sequence, contemplating the rest of the marks one after another, so that the mind's own eye opens into clarity, thereby breaking through the sunken, drowsy, dark mind; the merit of buddha-recollection then removes the offense obstructing the path. Question: if simply taking up a mark clearly is able to break through sunken dullness, why not instead practice the nine contemplations, the white bones, and the like? Answer: the nine contemplations and the white bones concern only this body of birth-and-death and its impurity — their power to remove offense is comparatively weak, and so they do not serve as the antidote here.

zh: 二、明治惡念思惟障者，障發如前說。對治，應教念佛功德。云何為念？正念之心緣佛十力、四無所畏、十八不共、一切種智圓照法界，常寂不動，普現色身，利益一切，功德無量，不可思議。如是念時，即是對治。何以故？此念佛功德從緣勝善法中生心數，惡念思惟從緣惡法中生心數。善能破惡，故應念報佛。譬如醜陋少智之人，在端正大智人中即自鄙恥。惡亦如是，在善心中則恥愧自息，緣佛功德，念念之中滅一切障。三、明治境界逼迫障者，罪業發相，如上所說。對治方法，應教念法佛。法佛者，即是法性平等，不生不滅，無有形色，空寂無為。無為之中既無境界，何者是逼迫之相？知境界空故，即是對治。若念三十二相，即非對治。何以故？是人未緣相時，已為境界惱亂，而更取相者，多因此著魔，狂亂其心。今觀空，破除諸境界，存心念佛，功德無量，即滅重罪。此為對治，於義可見。略說對治治竟。
en: Second, treating the obstruction of unwholesome, deliberate thought: the arising of this obstruction is as described above. Its antidote should teach recollecting the Buddha's own merit. What is meant by such recollection? A mind of right mindfulness taking as its object the Buddha's ten powers, four fearlessnesses, eighteen unshared qualities, and the wisdom that knows all things in every mode, illuminating the entire dharma-realm completely, forever still and unmoving, manifesting bodily forms everywhere, benefiting all beings, its merit measureless and inconceivable. Recollecting in this way is itself the antidote. Why is this? This merit of buddha-recollection gives rise to a mental factor arisen from taking the finest wholesome dharma as its object, whereas unwholesome, deliberate thought gives rise to a mental factor arisen from taking an unwholesome dharma as its object; the wholesome is able to overcome the unwholesome — hence one should recollect the reward-body buddha. It is like an ugly, unintelligent person who, standing among the handsome and greatly wise, feels ashamed of themselves of their own accord; the unwholesome is exactly the same — standing within a wholesome mind, it is ashamed and comes to rest of its own accord. Taking the Buddha's own merit as one's object, every obstruction is extinguished moment by moment.

Third, treating the obstruction of oppressive states: the mark of this karmic-offense arising is as described above. Its antidote method should teach recollecting the dharma-body buddha. The dharma-body is precisely the equality of the nature of dharmas itself, neither arising nor ceasing, without any form or shape, empty, still, and unconditioned. Within the unconditioned, there is no state present at all — what, then, could possibly be an oppressive mark? Knowing that every state is empty is itself the antidote. Were one instead to recollect the thirty-two marks, this would not serve as the antidote here. Why is this? Such a person, even before taking up any mark at all, has already been troubled and disturbed by these very states — and to take up a mark under these conditions risks, more often than not, becoming possessed by a demon through it, throwing the mind into further derangement. Here, instead, one contemplates emptiness, breaking through every state entirely, while still holding the mind fixed on buddha-recollection, whose merit is measureless — and grave offense is thereby extinguished. This is the antidote; its meaning can be readily seen. This concludes, in brief, the matched antidote treatment.

The fifteen matched antidotes map exactly onto the fifteen unwholesome marks and, in most cases, directly onto the fifteen wholesome-root gates already named in fascicle 3 — the treatise's basic move throughout this whole layer being to treat the practice that produces a wholesome mark as also the cure for its corresponding unwholesome one. Two details stand out: the aside on why the nine contemplations and white bones are the wrong antidote for karmic obstruction specifically (their power to remove offense is "comparatively weak"), and the warning against recollecting the thirty-two marks when oppressive states are already present, on the grounds that a practitioner already troubled by such states who then takes up a mark will, more often than not, become possessed by a demon through it — a rare case of the treatise naming a technique that is excellent in general but actively contraindicated for one particular ailment.

zh: 第二、明轉治者，出《摩訶衍論》解十力，明定力垢淨，智力中說。彼論云：「貪欲之人教修慈心，多瞋之人作不淨觀，愚癡多者教思惟邊無邊，掉散心中教令用智慧分別，沒心人中教令攝心。若如是者，名為轉治；若不爾者，名不轉治。」此為反上所說。今明轉治有二種：一者、病轉法亦轉；二者、病不轉而法轉。
en: Second, clarifying transposed treatment: this is given in the Mahāyāna treatise, in its explanation of the ten powers, within the discussion of the power of concentration's defilement and purity, and the power of wisdom. That treatise says: "One with much craving is taught to cultivate loving-kindness; one with much anger is taught the contemplation of impurity; one with much delusion is taught to contemplate the bounded and the unbounded; a scattered, agitated mind is taught to apply the discrimination of wisdom; and a sunken mind is taught to gather the mind in. If it is done in this way, it is called transposed treatment; if not, it is called non-transposed treatment." This runs contrary to what was said above. Here, transposed treatment is clarified as being of two kinds: the ailment itself is transposed and the dharma transposes along with it; or the ailment itself is not transposed while the dharma alone transposes.

zh: 今約前一觀中明轉治義，前對治治中，貪心多者，教觀不淨。觀心既成，見於不淨，厭患前境，便生瞋心。如佛在世，有諸比丘學不淨觀，成即顧人自害。如是之類，應教轉觀修慈，以治於瞋，名為轉治，此即藥病俱轉。如此說者，細熟尋檢，猶未稱教意。
en: Here, transposed treatment is first clarified with reference to a single contemplation as an example. Within the matched antidote treatment above, one with much craving was taught to contemplate impurity. Once this contemplation is accomplished, and impurity is genuinely seen, weariness and disgust arise toward the very object once desired, and an angry mind then arises instead — just as, while the Buddha was still in the world, there were monks who studied the contemplation of impurity and, upon its completion, hired others to take their lives. In such cases as these, one should be taught to shift the contemplation, cultivating loving-kindness instead, in order to treat this anger — this is called transposed treatment, the medicine transposing right along with the ailment itself. Stated in this way, however, upon careful and thorough examination, this still does not quite fit the teaching's true intent.

zh: 二者、病不轉而藥轉者，貪病不轉前不淨觀，修慈觀治。問曰：貪心之法，取人好相，慈亦取人好相，云何為對治？答曰：菩薩戒有明文：「一切男子皆是我父，一切女人皆是我母，而菩薩不起慈悲，行婬無度，不避六親，犯波羅夷罪。」若觀前境男女，皆如父、如母、如子，則自敬愛，心生慈念，能破貪欲，譬如父母，終不於子所生非法心。復次，慈名與他之樂，貪欲不善，增他煩惱，此非與樂之道。如是思惟，繫心修慈，慈定若發，即治貪欲。何以故？無量心是色界法，不應得有貪欲心生，此則病雖不轉，轉觀治之。今以不淨一門類之，餘十四門禪悉有二種轉治之義可知。復次，轉觀有二種：一者、轉心不轉境；二者、心境俱轉。善自推尋，其義可見。
en: Second, as for the ailment not transposing while the medicine alone transposes: the ailment of craving does not transpose, and yet, rather than continuing with the contemplation of impurity, loving-kindness is cultivated to treat it instead. Question: the dharma of a craving mind takes up another's attractive appearance as its object, and loving-kindness likewise takes up another's attractive appearance as its object — how, then, could this serve as an antidote at all? Answer: the bodhisattva precepts state explicitly: "Every man is my own father, and every woman is my own mother — and should a bodhisattva fail to give rise to loving-kindness and compassion, engaging in lust without restraint, showing no regard even for the six kinds of kin, this constitutes a pārājika offense." If one contemplates the man or woman before them as though each were truly one's own father, mother, or child, then a reverent affection arises of itself, the mind giving rise to a thought of loving-kindness able to break through craving — just as a parent, after all, never gives rise to any improper thought toward their own child. Furthermore, loving-kindness is precisely that which bestows happiness upon another, whereas craving, being unwholesome, only increases another's affliction — this is no path toward truly bestowing happiness at all. Reflecting in this way, fixing the mind on cultivating loving-kindness, once the concentration of loving-kindness is brought forth, craving is thereby treated. Why is this? The immeasurable minds are dharmas of the form realm, within which no craving mind ought to be able to arise at all — this, then, is a case where, although the ailment itself does not transpose, the contemplation is transposed instead to treat it.

Here, using the contemplation of impurity as a single example, the same twofold sense of transposed treatment should be understood to hold for the remaining fourteen gates of dhyāna as well. Furthermore, transposed contemplation is itself of two kinds: the mind is transposed while the object is not; or both mind and object are transposed together. This may be readily seen through careful reflection of one's own.

zh: 第三、明不轉治者，亦為二意：一者、病不轉，觀亦不轉；二者、病轉觀不轉。一、病不轉，觀亦不轉者，如貪心人作不淨觀，貪心不息，更增想作觀，不須轉觀，當更作膿血爛壞相等，作一人不息，復作多人，如是乃至一城、一聚落皆作不淨，如《禪經》中廣說。或進入白骨流光等治，貪心方息，故名不轉治。雖有此義，理而推之，猶恐未是教之正意。
en: Third, clarifying non-transposed treatment: this, too, has two senses — the ailment itself does not transpose and the contemplation does not transpose either; or the ailment itself transposes while the contemplation does not.

First, the ailment does not transpose and the contemplation does not transpose either: as when a person of much craving practices the contemplation of impurity, and the craving mind fails to come to rest — rather than shifting to a different contemplation, one instead intensifies the very same contemplation further: producing marks of pus, blood, and decay in still greater detail; if picturing a single corpse fails to bring it to rest, picturing many corpses instead; and so on, all the way to picturing an entire city or an entire village as equally impure, exactly as explained at length in the Chan Sūtra. Or one may progress further into the white bones and their flowing light as the treatment, until the craving mind finally comes to rest — this is called non-transposed treatment. Although this sense has its own validity, upon careful reflection, this, too, may not quite be the teaching's true intent.

zh: 二、病轉觀不轉治者，行者為有貪欲病，作不淨觀治，貪欲轉而生瞋恚，爾時不轉不淨觀，即於不淨中增想，作不淨觀及白骨流光入定，瞋心自除，亦得即為二意：一、境不轉而心轉；二、境不轉，心亦不轉。餘十四對治不轉治義，類亦如是。
en: Second, the ailment transposes while the contemplation does not: the practitioner, having the ailment of craving, practices the contemplation of impurity to treat it, and the craving then transposes into anger instead. At this point, rather than shifting away from the contemplation of impurity, one instead intensifies this very same contemplation further, practicing the contemplation of impurity together with the white bones and their flowing light to enter concentration, and the angry mind is thereby removed of itself. This, too, may be understood as two further senses: the object does not transpose while the mind does; or neither the object nor the mind transposes at all. The same pattern of non-transposed treatment should be understood to hold for the remaining fourteen antidotes as well.

The distinction between transposed and non-transposed treatment turns on a genuine clinical judgment call the treatise refuses to resolve with a single rule: when a practitioner's ailment shifts mid-treatment (craving curdling into anger, say), should the antidote shift to match the new symptom, or should the original practice simply be intensified until it works through the new symptom as well? Both are illustrated with the same starting case (craving treated by the contemplation of impurity) so the two can be compared directly — yet Zhiyi qualifies both: of the first sense of transposed treatment he says that, on careful examination, it "still does not quite fit the teaching's true intent," and of the first sense of non-transposed treatment that it, too, "may not quite be the teaching's true intent." The section is a reminder that the fifteen matched antidotes just given are a starting point for a teacher's judgment, not a rigid lookup table.

quiz.q: Why is counting the breath taught for discursive thought in a sharp, lucid mind?
options: counting fixes the mind on the breath, the remedy for disorder; it keeps count in a settled, deliberate mind, which treats sharp restlessness
quiz.why: "In the method of counting the breath, the mind is fixed upon the breath, and the breath is the true medicine for treating disorder ... The method of counting the breath keeps count within a settled, deliberate mind, and a settled, deliberate mind is able to treat sharp restlessness."

quiz.q: Why is following the breath taught for half-lucid, half-dull discursive thought, rather than counting or observing alone?
options: counting alone encourages dullness, observing alone encourages restlessness; following the breath breaks both
quiz.why: "As the fine breath goes out and comes in, the mind, sustained by following it, is thereby able to break through discursive thought ... able thereby to break through dullness and sinking as well ... Were one to use counting the breath alone, there would be the fault of encouraging dullness; were one to use observing the breath alone, there would be the fault of encouraging restlessness."

quiz.q: For discursive thought in a dull mind, observing the breath is taught. How?
options: observe where the entering breath comes from, its course, and where it rests; going out it does not scatter, coming in it does not accumulate
quiz.why: "As the breath enters, one closely observes exactly where this breath comes from, what course it travels through in between, and where it finally comes to rest upon entering ... Tracing the breath back to its very root source in this way, one finds that, going out, it does not scatter, and, coming in, it does not accumulate."

quiz.q: What is the antidote for one with much external craving?
options: the nine contemplations: taking up the mark of a corpse at the charnel ground — swollen, decaying, pus, worms
quiz.why: "The antidote method should teach the practice of the nine contemplations: going, if possible, to a charnel ground to take up the mark of an actual corpse ... reflecting that what I myself am so attached to is exactly the same as this." The first liberation treats inner-and-outer craving, and the great contemplation pervasive craving.

quiz.q: What treats craving both external and internal?
options: the first liberation: seeing the inner body as impure breaks inner craving, seeing the outer as impure removes outer craving
quiz.why: "One should be taught to practice the first liberation and its related contemplations, closely observing the inner body as impure, decaying, and repugnant, thereby breaking through craving that takes the inward body as its object; and, as before, observing the outward body as impure and repugnant as well."

quiz.q: What treats deviant anger?
options: loving-kindness toward beings: taking a loved one's happiness as object, then extending happiness even to enemies
quiz.why: "To treat it, one should be led to cultivate loving-kindness that takes sentient beings as its object, taking up the mark of a single loved one's happiness and taking this as the object through which concentration is entered." Loving-kindness toward dharma treats anger in accord with reason, and objectless loving-kindness anger through disputation.

quiz.q: Why is anger in accord with reason treated by loving-kindness toward dharma?
options: seeing the aggregates as empty, no being is seen, so there is no keeping or breaking, right or wrong; with right and wrong dissolved, anger rests
quiz.why: "One should be taught to cultivate loving-kindness that takes dharma as its object, contemplating the five aggregates as empty and unreal, so that no sentient being is seen at all — how, then, could there be any matter of upholding or violating, right or wrong, to speak of? ... Once right and wrong have dissolved away in this manner, the angry mind comes to rest of itself."

quiz.q: Why is objectless loving-kindness cultivated for anger through disputation?
options: such a person relies on some position, even the middle way, and so disputes; objectless loving-kindness cuts off language and recollects nothing, so nothing is left to dispute
quiz.why: "Clinging, perhaps, to one of the four propositions or to their total negation, or even clinging to the middle way itself. In every such case there is something relied upon ... in practicing this loving-kindness, the path of language is cut off ... If there is nothing recalled or dwelt upon, on what basis could contention give rise to an angry mind at all?"

quiz.q: "One with much delusion should contemplate causation" — what kind of person is meant by delusion here?
options: not the dullness of oxen or sheep, but an intelligent, sharp person who reasons yet lacks right wisdom, grasping principle with a deviant mind
quiz.why: "What is meant here by 'delusion' does not refer to something like an ox or a sheep; rather, it refers to a person of genuine intelligence and sharp faculties who nonetheless, in discriminating and reasoning things through, fails to attain right wisdom, seizing upon principle instead with a deviant mind."

quiz.q: Treating annihilationism and eternalism with the twelve links across three times, how are the twelve distributed?
options: two in the past, eight in the present, two in the future
quiz.why: "The antidote method should teach the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination across the three periods of time: two links belong to the past, eight to the present, and two to the future."

quiz.q: The verse "Within my true Buddhadharma, though empty, it is not cut off" continues how?
options: continuing, it is not permanent; good and evil are never lost
quiz.why: "Within my own true Buddhadharma, though empty, it is nonetheless not cut off; / Continuing on, it is nonetheless not permanent; the wholesome and unwholesome are nonetheless never lost."

quiz.q: Which provisional reality does each of the three twelve-link contemplations break through?
options: three times breaks continuity; karmic result breaks establishment by cause; single thought breaks mutual dependence
quiz.why: The three-times contemplation "may likewise serve as the antidote breaking through the delusion of provisional reality established by continuity"; the karmic-result contemplation breaks "the delusion of provisional reality established by cause"; and the single-thought contemplation breaks "the delusion of provisional reality established by mutual dependence."

quiz.q: Why does the single-thought twelve-link contemplation break the view of a fixed worldly nature?
options: a single thought contains all twelve; one is not twelve nor twelve one; the one has no fixed nature, so no fixed worldly nature can be found
quiz.why: "The practitioner deeply contemplates that, within a single thought-moment, all twelve links are already present in full: the one is not the twelve, and the twelve are not the one ... One should know that the one has no fixed nature of its own — and, since there is no fixed 'one,' no fixed worldly nature can be found either."

quiz.q: What is the antidote for the obstruction of sunken, dark dullness?
options: take one of the response-body buddha's thirty-two marks, such as the tuft between the brows, eyes closed; if unclear, look at an image and close again, then contemplate the marks in turn
quiz.why: "Its antidote should teach taking up, from among the thirty-two marks of the response-body buddha, any single mark as its object — perhaps first taking the mark of the tuft of hair between the Buddha's brows, closing the eyes and contemplating it ... If it remains unclear, one should open the eyes and look again, then close them once more."

quiz.q: If taking up a clear mark breaks dullness, why not use the nine contemplations or white bones?
options: they concern only the impure body of birth-and-death; their power to remove offense is weak
quiz.why: "The nine contemplations and the white bones concern only this body of birth-and-death and its impurity — their power to remove offense is comparatively weak, and so they do not serve as the antidote here."

quiz.q: For the obstruction of oppressive states, which buddha should be recollected?
options: the dharma-body: equality of dharma-nature, unarisen, formless, empty and unconditioned; knowing states to be empty is the antidote
quiz.why: "Its antidote method should teach recollecting the dharma-body buddha. The dharma-body is precisely the equality of the nature of dharmas itself, neither arising nor ceasing, without any form or shape, empty, still, and unconditioned ... Knowing that every state is empty is itself the antidote."

quiz.q: Why is recollecting the thirty-two marks not the antidote for oppressive states?
options: already disturbed by states before taking up any mark, taking a mark often leads to possession and derangement
quiz.why: "Were one instead to recollect the thirty-two marks, this would not serve as the antidote here. Why is this? Such a person, even before taking up any mark at all, has already been troubled and disturbed by these very states — and to take up a mark under these conditions risks, more often than not, becoming possessed by a demon through it."

quiz.q: Where does "transposed treatment" come from, and what does the cited passage say?
options: the Mahāyāna treatise on the ten powers: the craving taught loving-kindness, the angry impurity, the deluded the bounded and unbounded
quiz.why: "This is given in the Mahāyāna treatise, in its explanation of the ten powers ... That treatise says: 'One with much craving is taught to cultivate loving-kindness; one with much anger is taught the contemplation of impurity; one with much delusion is taught to contemplate the bounded and the unbounded ... If it is done in this way, it is called transposed treatment.'"

quiz.q: What are the two kinds of transposed treatment?
options: the ailment transposes and the dharma too; the ailment does not transpose but the dharma does
quiz.why: "Here, transposed treatment is clarified as being of two kinds: the ailment itself is transposed and the dharma transposes along with it; or the ailment itself is not transposed while the dharma alone transposes." Mind and object are the two kinds of transposed contemplation.

quiz.q: When craving is treated by loving-kindness, someone objects that both take another's attractive appearance. How does the text answer?
options: citing the bodhisattva precepts — every man my father, every woman my mother — seeing others as parents and children gives rise to reverent kindness that breaks craving
quiz.why: "The bodhisattva precepts state explicitly: 'Every man is my own father, and every woman is my own mother' ... If one contemplates the man or woman before them as though each were truly one's own father, mother, or child, then a reverent affection arises of itself, the mind giving rise to a thought of loving-kindness able to break through craving."

quiz.q: Once the concentration of loving-kindness arises, why does it treat craving?
options: the immeasurable minds are form-realm dharmas, where craving should not arise
kindness makes one dislike the other
quiz.why: "Once the concentration of loving-kindness is brought forth, craving is thereby treated. Why is this? The immeasurable minds are dharmas of the form realm, within which no craving mind ought to be able to arise at all."

quiz.q: Transposed contemplation is itself of which two kinds?
options: the mind transposes but not the object; both mind and object transpose
quiz.why: "Transposed contemplation is itself of two kinds: the mind is transposed while the object is not; or both mind and object are transposed together." The ailment-and-dharma pair describes the two kinds of transposed treatment.

quiz.q: In "neither the ailment nor the contemplation transposes," what does one do?
options: without shifting, intensify the same contemplation — more detail, many corpses, a whole city, or on to the white bones' flowing light
quiz.why: "As when a person of much craving practices the contemplation of impurity, and the craving mind fails to come to rest — rather than shifting to a different contemplation, one instead intensifies the very same contemplation further ... all the way to picturing an entire city or an entire village as equally impure."

quiz.q: What is the example of the ailment transposing but the contemplation not?
options: impurity treats craving, craving turns to anger, yet one intensifies the same contemplation to the flowing light, and anger falls away
craving turns to anger, switch to kindness
quiz.why: "The craving then transposes into anger instead. At this point, rather than shifting away from the contemplation of impurity, one instead intensifies this very same contemplation further, practicing the contemplation of impurity together with the white bones and their flowing light to enter concentration, and the angry mind is thereby removed of itself."
